paragraphs.source_en: This yawn of the master's was again like the distant baying of a whale, quite extraordinarily out of the common run. After the yawn had run its course, the master leisurely put on his clothes and then went off to the bathroom to wash his face. His wife, who had been waiting impatiently, at once folded up the bedding and began the usual sweeping and cleaning. The cleaning was the same old routine as ever, and the master's way of washing his face was likewise the same old routine, unchanged these ten years. As I have mentioned before, it was the customary gargling and tooth-brushing with his ga-ga and ge-ge noises. Then, having parted his hair and slung a towel over his shoulder, he made his august progress into the dining room and seated himself loftily beside the oblong brazier. When I say oblong brazier, some of you will no doubt picture one made of oak with a fish-scale grain, or a four-legged affair wholly sheathed in copper, with a pretty young woman, her glossy hair freshly washed, sitting beside it with one knee drawn up and tapping her long pipe on its rosewood rim. But the oblong brazier belonging to our Mr. Kushami is by no means any such stylish article. What material it is actually made of is hard for an amateur to judge; at any rate, it is an object of extreme antique elegance. A proper oblong brazier generally displays its worth only when it has been polished until it shines. But as for this odd contrivance of the master's, whether it is oak, cherry, or paulownia is not only unclear, it has almost never been touched with a wiping cloth, so that it presents a thoroughly black and gloomy appearance. As for where such a thing was bought, it was not bought at all. Then was it given to him by someone? No one, surely, would have been willing to give him a brazier. If so, then, should one press him and ask whether he stole it? The answer becomes vague and evasive. It seems that long ago there was an old retired relative of his; for a time after the old man died, the master had been asked to look after the vacant house, and later, when he married, set up his own household, and moved out, he absentmindedly brought along the brazier he had been using there as if it were his own. This was, one must admit, rather a shabby proceeding. Yet when one thinks it over, shabby though it is, such things occur quite often in the world. Bankers, for example, handle other people's money every day, and as they handle it over and over, other people's money comes to look just like their own. Officials are by nature servants of the people; they are no different from agents entrusted with certain powers so that they may conduct people's business for them. Yet while making use of the entrusted authority and dealing with affairs day after day, they fall under the delusion that this is power they themselves possess, and that the people have no right whatever to interfere with it. Since people of this sort are numerous in society, one naturally ought not to take the oblong-brazier affair as proof that the master has a thievish disposition. If my master has a thievish disposition, then everyone under heaven has a thievish disposition too.

units.source_zh: 当官的本来是人民的公仆，这和为了让人替自己办事，委任给一定权限的代理人并没有什么两样。

units.source_en: Yet while making use of the entrusted authority and dealing with affairs day after day, they fall under the delusion that this is power they themselves possess, and that the people have no right whatever to interfere with it.
units.source_zh: 可是，在利用被委托的权力和一天一天处理事务当中就会产生错觉：这是自己拥有的权力，人民对此根本无权过问。

units.source_en: Since people of this sort are numerous in society, one naturally ought not to take the oblong-brazier affair as proof that the master has a thievish disposition.

units.source_en: If my master has a thievish disposition, then everyone under heaven has a thievish disposition too.

paragraphs.source_zh: 主人的这个呵欠声又恍如鲸鱼的远吠，颇为不同凡响。打呵欠告一段落之后，主人慢条斯理地穿好衣服，然后到洗澡间洗脸去了。主人的妻子等得好不耐烦，立刻叠好被褥，又开始了打扫。打扫照旧是老一套，而主人洗脸的方式也十年如一日，仍是老一套。正像前边我讲过的那样，照例是他那套嘎嘎、咯咯的刷牙漱口。然后，分好了头，肩上搭一条毛巾，起驾来到餐厅，超然地坐在长火盆的旁边。我一提到长火盆，诸位准会想象那火盆是用带鱼鳞木纹的橡木制成的，或是四脚落地式的用全铜包镶的，一个刚洗完青丝的俏丽少妇支着一条腿儿坐在火盆旁边，在火盆的紫檀沿儿上，砰砰地磕着长管烟袋的光景吧。我们这位苦沙弥先生的长火盆可够不上那种风流的玩意儿。它到底是用什么材料做的，外行人很难判断，反正是件非常古雅的东西。考究的长火盆一般是必须把它擦拭得精光锃亮才显示出它的身份。但主人这件怪里怪气的玩意儿，是橡木做的还是樱木做的，或者是桐木做的呢，不仅身份不明，而且几乎从来未用抹布揩拭过，因此看去，给人一种黑黢黢的感觉。说到这种东西是从哪儿买的，它根本就不是买来的。那么是别人送他的吗？也不会有人肯送他火盆吧。既然这样，那么追问他是偷来的吗？回答又是含含糊糊。原来以前他亲戚中有个老人，那老人死后一段时期，他曾给那家看守过空房子，以后他自己结婚安了家，从那所房子搬出来的时候，便糊里糊涂将他在那里当做自己东西使用过的火盆也带来了。这种做法未免有点恶劣。不过仔细想来，恶劣是恶劣，但这种事儿世上是经常有的。比如银行家这种人，每天总在摆弄别人的钱，摆弄来摆弄去，别人的钱就会变成和自己的钱一样。当官的本来是人民的公仆，这和为了让人替自己办事，委任给一定权限的代理人并没有什么两样。可是，在利用被委托的权力和一天一天处理事务当中就会产生错觉：这是自己拥有的权力，人民对此根本无权过问。既然这种人在社会上很多，当然就不应该将长火盆事件看作是主人具有的小偷习性。如果我家主人带有小偷的习性，那么天下的人也都带有小偷的习性了。

paragraphs.source_en: The master took up his position beside the oblong brazier and sat facing the dining table; on the other three sides were already assembled the Little One, whose face had just been washed with a wiping cloth, Tonko, who goes to the Ocha-no-Miso school, and Sunko, who had stuck her fingers into the face-powder bottle, and all were eating breakfast together. The master first looked over the faces of the three young ladies with impartial attention. Tonko's face has the long oval outline of the guard of a Nanban iron sword. As for the second daughter, Sunko, being the younger sister she does somewhat preserve her elder sister's cast of features, yet she quite suggests a bright red tray finished in Ryukyu lacquer. But the Little One, in particular, shines with a distinction all her own: she has a long face. If it were long vertically, there would be no shortage of examples in the world; but this little creature's face is stretched out sideways. However changeable the fashions of the world may be, surely a face elongated sideways will never come into style. The master, though they are his own children, has often pondered them carefully: one way or another, they must gradually grow up. Far from merely growing gradually, the speed of their growth is like bamboo shoots in a Zen temple turning into young bamboo in the twinkling of an eye; they grow larger and larger. Each time the master feels, They have grown again, he is also deeply uneasy, as though someone were pressing close behind him in pursuit. For all the master's vagueness and impracticality, he does at least know that these three young ladies are, after all, female. Since they are female, he also understands that sooner or later he must somehow marry them off. That much common sense he still possesses. Precisely because he understands this, he is also clearly aware that he lacks the ability to get them married. Thus, though they are his own children, he feels them to be a considerable burden. If he was going to find them a burden, how much better it would have been not to have had these children in the first place. Yet that is precisely what humans are: if one were to define man, it would be enough simply to say that he is a creature who goes out of his way to do unnecessary things and thereby makes trouble for himself.
